sections.h2: What makes selling a house in Ann Arbor different?
sections.html:
Ann Arbor is a college-town market with high prices, a low owner-occupancy rate and a large renter population, so the buyer pool for a house differs from most Michigan cities. The Census Bureau reports a median owner-occupied value of $453,400 for 2020 to 2024, and only 45.5 percent of homes are occupied by their owners.

The city is the seat of Washtenaw County and sits on the Huron River, with the University of Michigan at its center. Wikipedia counts 123,851 residents in the 2020 census, and the Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate is 122,233. The city covers 28.20 square miles of land, and about 65 percent of residents lived in the same house a year earlier, which is a lower figure than in most suburbs around Detroit.

A seller here usually weighs three routes: listing with an agent, selling directly to an investor or other cash buyer, or selling to a tenant or neighbor. Each route still runs through the same recording, transfer tax and assessor steps described below.

sections.h2: How do jobs, schools and roads affect Ann Arbor home values?
sections.html:
The University of Michigan employs about 30,000 people, roughly 12,000 of them at the medical center, and that payroll holds up demand for housing near campus and downtown. Health services, research labs and technology companies add jobs, and the area also includes federal research sites such as a NOAA laboratory and an EPA vehicle emissions laboratory.

Public schools belong to Ann Arbor Public Schools, whose high schools are Pioneer, Huron, Skyline and Community, and the district enrolled 17,070 students in 2021 to 2022. Concordia University Ann Arbor and several private and charter schools sit in the city as well. The Census Bureau puts the share of adults with a bachelor's degree or higher at 77.9 percent.

  • US-23 runs along the eastern edge, M-14 along the north, and I-94 along the south and west.
  • TheRide, run by the Ann Arbor Area Transportation Authority, provides local bus service.
  • Amtrak's Wolverine train stops at the Ann Arbor station on the Chicago to Pontiac route.
  • The city has more than 160 parks and about 50,000 street trees, which is how it earned the Tree Town nickname.

Hills near the Huron River and mature trees give many streets a settled look, and a house near a park or the river often shows well in photos.

sections.h2: What does the Census say about Ann Arbor's housing market?
sections.html:
The Census figures for 2020 to 2024 show a high-cost, high-turnover market where renters outnumber owners. The table below sets out the main housing and income measures for the city.

Ann Arbor housing and income figures, Census Bureau QuickFacts

For sellers, the figure to watch is the owner-occupied rate. With owners in fewer than half of homes, a good share of Ann Arbor houses are held as rentals, so expect some buyers to ask about rental licensing before they ask about the roof.

sections.h2: How much will the Michigan transfer tax cost on an Ann Arbor sale?
sections.html:
The seller pays $8.60 for every $1,000 of sale price in combined state and county transfer tax when the deed is recorded with the Washtenaw County Register of Deeds. State law sets the state rate at $3.75 per $500 and the county rate at 55 cents per $500 for counties of fewer than 2,000,000 people.

On a $450,000 sale, the tax works out to $3,870, since the sale holds 900 units of $500 at $4.30 each. Recording itself costs $30 per document under MCL 600.2567, although a charter county may set its own schedule, so ask the Washtenaw office for its current fee table. The county site carries a fee schedule, a Michigan real estate transfer tax page and an eRecording page.

A warranty deed also needs a tax certificate from the county treasurer before recording. Some transfers are exempt, including deeds that carry less than $100 in consideration and conveyances from a parent to a child or from a grandparent to a grandchild under the state act. Cite the exemption on the deed when one applies.

sections.h2: Can a buyer run a short-term rental from an Ann Arbor house?
sections.html:
Only with a city license, and the rules limit who qualifies. Ann Arbor's short-term rental ordinance, Chapter 97, covers any stay of 30 consecutive days or fewer, and the license costs $500 per unit per year.

  • In residential zones, only the owner's principal residence can be licensed, and a sworn statement of principal residency goes with the application.
  • Accessory dwelling units cannot be used as short-term rentals.
  • Third-party companies cannot hold a license.
  • Non-owner-occupied properties in the zones that allow them need a valid Certificate of Compliance first.
  • Applications are filed and paid online through the city's STREAM portal, review can take up to 21 business days, and denied applications are not refunded.

This matters when you sell, because an investor who sees an Ann Arbor house as a short-term rental may learn the zoning does not allow it. Be ready to answer that question from a prospective buyer, and point them to the city's planning page for the zone table. Long-term rentals are a separate program. The city also has a Green Rental Housing program that uses an energy score of 110 or below on a HERS assessment, so a buyer who plans to rent the house long term should ask the city whether that standard applies.

sections.h2: What does the Ann Arbor assessor handle after a sale?
sections.html:
The Ann Arbor Assessor's Office, on the fifth floor of Larcom City Hall at 301 E. Huron St., takes the Property Transfer Affidavit, the Principal Residence Exemption affidavit and the request to rescind an exemption. Forms can be filed in person, by mail or through the city's online submission page, and the office can be reached at 734.794.6530.

Michigan requires the new owner to file the transfer affidavit within 45 days of the sale. Sellers should rescind their own exemption on the home they are leaving, and a buyer who will live in the house claims it with the state form.

Property taxes are the product of millage rates and taxable value, and more than half of the city's revenue comes from them. Taxable value rises each year by the Inflation Rate Multiplier or 5 percent, whichever is less, until a sale resets it. Notices of assessment go out in early March. The Board of Review meets starting the Monday of the third week of March for four days, and a residential appeal to the Michigan Tax Tribunal is due by July 31. A buyer who closes in the spring should check the notice date before the Board of Review window closes.

faqs.q: How much is the transfer tax in Ann Arbor?
faqs.a: It is $8.60 per $1,000 of the sale price, paid by the seller at recording. That covers $7.50 of state tax and $1.10 of county tax, so a $450,000 sale owes $3,870.

faqs.q: Which office records a deed for an Ann Arbor property?
faqs.a: The Washtenaw County Register of Deeds records it. Warranty deeds need a county treasurer tax certificate first, and the recording fee is $30 per document under state law unless the county's own schedule differs.

faqs.q: Do I need a rental license to sell a house with tenants in Ann Arbor?
faqs.a: Selling does not need a license, but a buyer who intends to rent must follow the city's rental rules. A short-term rental needs a $500 annual license, and non-owner-occupied units need a Certificate of Compliance.

faqs.q: When can I appeal an Ann Arbor assessment?
faqs.a: The City Board of Review meets starting the Monday of the third week of March for four days, and that is when you must appeal. A residential owner then has until July 31 to appeal to the Michigan Tax Tribunal.

faqs.q: What form tells the assessor I sold my Ann Arbor home?
faqs.a: The buyer files a Property Transfer Affidavit within 45 days. You file a Request to Rescind Principal Residence Exemption, Form 2602, if you claimed the exemption on the house you sold.
